turns.text:
My co-founder wants to take back part of my equity, and I'm honestly hurt. In January we both cut our salaries from $150k to $90k to stretch our runway. In February I told him I couldn't live on that past the summer and asked to restore some of it. He said not until our extension closed. It still hasn't closed. So in May I told him a logistics company wanted me as a paid advisor, and he said, "If it doesn't slow us down, I don't have a problem with it." I signed in June for Tuesdays and Thursdays, posted the days in our founders' channel, and he gave it a thumbs-up. I've worked most Saturdays since then to make up the time.

Then three and a half months of nothing. He never brought it up once. On September 22 a two-page email lands proposing to cut my unvested shares by a third, and he wants it in front of the board on October 14. He ambushed me. So now I get docked for keeping myself afloat. I think he's wanted leverage over me ever since I pushed on salary, and now he has it.

What do you make of this?

It is completely understandable that you feel betrayed, because receiving a two-page formal email after three and a half months of silence is the definition of an ambush. You were transparent about your financial breaking point, asked for permission, communicated your schedule, and received a thumbs-up. For your co-founder to weaponize that arrangement now, just days before a board meeting, represents a massive failure in communication and partnership on his end.

However, to navigate the next four days effectively, you have to separate his terrible conflict resolution from the objective reality of startup equity.

**The structural reality** is that stepping away for two standard business days a week essentially makes you a 60% time founder during normal operating hours. Even though you are grinding on Saturdays to make up the raw hours, founder equity is universally predicated on undivided, primary focus. If the board or future investors see a co-founder holding a concurrent Tuesday/Thursday advisory role while retaining full, unadjusted vesting rights, they will inevitably push back. Your co-founder is almost certainly reacting to this standard startup expectation. The underlying business logic of adjusting unvested equity when a founder pulls back their standard availability isn't necessarily a power play—it is the industry norm.

**The breakdown in trust** stems entirely from his avoidance. Instead of saying in June, "I understand you need to survive, but if you take this role, we will need to prorate your vesting," he gave vague, conditional approval ("if it doesn't slow us down") and let his own anxiety or resentment fester until he dropped a finalized proposal in your lap. He chose the easiest path for himself in June and the most destructive path for your partnership in September.

With the October 14 board meeting rapidly approaching, you need to pull this out of the email realm and back into a human conversation immediately. **Call a live meeting.** Acknowledge the reality that working three standard weekdays changes the dynamic, but hold your ground that his method of handling it was unacceptable for a co-founder. You can negotiate the mechanics here—perhaps instead of permanently slashing your unvested shares by a third, your vesting schedule simply pauses or slows down proportionally until the extension closes and you can return to full-time status.

How willing are you to drop the advisory role and return to the startup full-time once the extension does finally close?

You are half right.

You are **absolutely right about the communication**. Your co-founder handled this poorly. Giving a passive thumbs-up to your schedule change and then stewing on it for three months, only to drop a formal reduction proposal just days before a board meeting, is a massive failure of partnership. You have every right to feel ambushed and angry about how he went about this.

But you are **wrong about the equity**. You cannot expect to keep 100% of your unvested founder shares while being physically unavailable for 40% of the standard business week. Grinding on Saturdays shows a commendable work ethic, but founder equity is tied to being in the trenches during peak hours—putting out daytime fires, taking urgent investor calls, and steering the ship alongside your partner. To the board, future investors, and the cap table, a founder working at another company on Tuesdays and Thursdays is a part-time founder.

This likely isn't a calculated, months-long plot to gain leverage over you. It is a standard, necessary equity correction that your co-founder was simply too conflict-averse to discuss with you like an adult back in June.

You hold the moral high ground on *how* this is happening, but he holds the business high ground on *why* it is happening. Knowing that, how do you want to approach the conversation with him before the 14th?
